title: Is any man sick (James 5:13–16)
hook: call the priests to anoint the sick: the Church's root for anointing

segments.voice: Yesterday, faith without works: a body with no breath. Your line was faith that works. Which belief got its action? Day six hundred seven.

Many parish priests carry a small metal case, about the size of a lipstick, with a screw-top lid. Inside is a bit of cotton soaked in olive oil, blessed by the bishop during Holy Week. It rides in a coat pocket or a car glove box for months. Then one night the phone rings: a hospital, a nursing home, a kitchen where someone's father has taken a turn. The priest drives over, takes out the little case, and does something Christians have done since the first century. The instructions come from the end of the letter of James.
screen: `A SMALL METAL CASE OF OIL.` → `THE PHONE RINGS AT NIGHT.` → `INSTRUCTIONS FROM JAMES.`

segments.voice: James is wrapping up his letter, and he covers the whole range of life in three quick questions. Is anyone sad? Let him pray. Is anyone cheerful? Let him sing. And then, in the Douay-Rheims: "Is any man sick among you? Let him bring in the priests of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord." Notice who moves first. The sick person calls. Nobody is meant to suffer quietly in a back room so as not to be a bother. James goes on: "And the prayer of faith shall save the sick man: and the Lord shall raise him up: and if he be in sins, they shall be forgiven him." The Greek word for those priests is presbyteroi, elders, and our English word priest grows out of it. The Catholic Church sees in these verses the root of a sacrament, the Anointing of the Sick. The Council of Trent taught that it was hinted at in Mark's Gospel, where the twelve anointed many sick people with oil, and made known by James. For centuries it was mostly given at the very end of life and called Extreme Unction, the last anointing. After the Second Vatican Council the Church stressed its older name and wider use: anyone seriously ill, someone facing major surgery, the frail elderly, and it can be received more than once. The priest lays his hands on the person in silence, then anoints the forehead and the hands. The Church doesn't promise a cure. It speaks of strength, peace and courage, and of bodily healing too, if God wills it. Saved and raised up can mean more than one thing.
screen: `SAD? PRAY. CHEERFUL? SING.` · `THE SICK PERSON CALLS.` · `PRESBYTEROI: THE ELDERS.` · `FROM LAST RITES TO ANOINTING OF THE SICK.` · then, large: `THE PRAYER OF FAITH SHALL SAVE THE SICK MAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for someone sick, or hold them in mind. Sit comfortably and breathe slowly. Bring to mind one person who is ill right now: in the hospital, at home, or carrying something no one can see. Picture them as clearly as you can, where they are, how they're sitting or lying. If it feels right, imagine your hand resting gently on their shoulder. If you pray, you can pray for them by name, in your own words or with a prayer you know. If you don't, just stay with them in your thoughts and wish them strength and peace. The bell holds the time.
Is any man sick. James five: call the priests of the church to pray over the sick and anoint them. For Catholics, the root of the Anointing of the Sick. Today's word.
Your line: the prayer of faith. Today, let the person you held in mind know they're thought of: a message, a call, a visit. Day six hundred seven.

howItsDone: In the sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick, a priest prays over a seriously ill or elderly person, lays hands on them in silence and anoints their forehead and hands with oil blessed by the bishop; families can ask their parish or a hospital chaplain for it.

fork.setup: you're sick, and you belong to the church James is writing to. you don't want to be a bother. what does James tell you to do?
options: suffer quietly and wait to get better.
call in the priests of the church to pray over you and anoint you.
travel to wherever the apostles are.
fork.reveal: James puts the first move in the sick person's hands: let him bring in the priests. nobody is meant to suffer alone in a back room.

original.note: Greek: elders (James 5:14). the English word priest comes from it, through Latin presbyter.

trapdoor: what you thought: last rites, the thing a priest does when someone is about to die.
what it means: the Anointing of the Sick, for anyone seriously ill or frail, with prayer, laying on of hands and oil, for strength and healing.
what a scholar hears: Trent taught the sacrament was hinted at in Mark 6:13 and made known in James 5:14–15; Vatican II restored the wider name and use.

sources.ref: Council of Trent, Session 14 (1551), on Extreme Unction; Sacrosanctum Concilium 73; Catechism of the Catholic Church 1510–1523

notes: James 5:13 paraphrased ('Is anyone sad? Let him pray. Is anyone cheerful? Let him sing'). Douay-Rheims reads approximately 'Is any of you sad? Let him pray. Is he cheerful in mind? Let him sing.' Not quoted.
Oil stock description and oil of the sick blessed by the bishop at the Chrism Mass during Holy Week. Confirm the details (priests may also bless oil in case of necessity).
Trent (Session 14) on the sacrament 'insinuated' by Mark 6:13 and 'promulgated' by James (CCC 1511). Paraphrased as 'hinted at' and 'made known'. Confirm.
Vatican II (Sacrosanctum Concilium 73) on the name 'anointing of the sick'; the sacrament can be repeated (CCC 1515); it is not only for those at the point of death (CCC 1514). Confirm.
The rite: silent laying on of hands; anointing of forehead and hands (Latin rite). Confirm.
'Since the first century' for anointing the sick rests on Mark 6:13 and James 5. Confirm the phrasing.
